evidence_excerpts: A continuously differentiable function is $L$-smooth, for some $L>0$, when its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean norm:

\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|,
\qquad \forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.
The same positive constant must work for every pair of points in the whole domain, and both norms are Euclidean.

evidence_excerpts: The key consequence is the Descent Lemma. If $f$ is $L$-smooth, then for every $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d$,

f(y)\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle
+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|^2.
The coefficient of the squared displacement is one half of the smoothness constant.
